note: A curated subset covering the techniques a web-application weakness plausibly maps to. Not the full matrix. Regenerate/extend from the official STIX bundle when attack_validate needs full coverage.

techniques.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to gain initial access to a network. This includes injection flaws, SSRF, insecure deserialization, XXE and any bug in a public web application or API.

techniques.name: External Remote Services
techniques.description: Adversaries may leverage external-facing remote services (VPNs, admin consoles, remote desktop gateways) to initially access or persist within a network.

techniques.name: Valid Accounts
techniques.description: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts to gain access, escalate privileges, persist, or evade defences. Covers authentication-bypass and account-takeover outcomes on a web application.

techniques.name: Valid Accounts: Default Accounts
techniques.description: Adversaries may use default account credentials shipped with an application or appliance to gain access.

techniques.name: Valid Accounts: Local Accounts
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse local accounts configured on a host or application for access and privilege escalation.

techniques.name: Brute Force
techniques.description: Adversaries may use brute force to guess credentials or secrets when the application does not rate-limit or lock out authentication attempts.

techniques.name: Brute Force: Password Guessing
techniques.description: Adversaries may guess passwords against a login endpoint without prior knowledge of the password.

techniques.name: Brute Force: Password Spraying
techniques.description: Adversaries may try a small set of common passwords across many accounts to avoid lockout.

techniques.name: Brute Force: Credential Stuffing
techniques.description: Adversaries may use credentials from prior breaches against a login endpoint that does not detect automated reuse.

techniques.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
techniques.description: Adversaries may exploit a software vulnerability to collect credentials — e.g. a bug that discloses password hashes, reset tokens, or enables user enumeration.

techniques.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
techniques.description: Adversaries may steal web application or service session cookies to authenticate as a user without needing the password — via XSS, an over-permissive CORS policy, or token disclosure.

techniques.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie
techniques.description: Adversaries may use a stolen or fixed web session cookie to authenticate to a web application, bypassing normal authentication.

techniques.name: Unsecured Credentials
techniques.description: Adversaries may search compromised systems, application responses, or client-side code to find insecurely stored credentials, API keys and tokens.

techniques.name: Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
techniques.description: Adversaries may read files (config, backups, source) that contain credentials, reachable through path traversal or misconfiguration.

techniques.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse command and script interpreters to execute commands or code, often the end state of an injection or deserialization bug.

techniques.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse Unix shell commands, e.g. via OS command injection in a web application that passes input to a shell.

techniques.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Python
techniques.description: Adversaries may execute Python code, e.g. via unsafe pickle deserialization or server-side template injection in a Python stack.

techniques.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: JavaScript
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse JavaScript execution in a victim's browser (XSS) or server-side (Node.js), for example through reflected, stored or DOM cross-site scripting.

techniques.name: Server Software Component: Web Shell
techniques.description: Adversaries may plant a web shell on a server — typically via an unrestricted file-upload vulnerability — for persistent command execution over HTTP.

techniques.name: Exploitation for Defense Evasion
techniques.description: Adversaries may exploit a vulnerability to bypass or disable a security control — a WAF, an authorization check, an input filter.

techniques.name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism
techniques.description: Adversaries may circumvent mechanisms designed to control privilege — e.g. setting a hidden 'isAdmin' field via mass assignment, or reaching an admin-only function without the role.

techniques.name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
techniques.description: Adversaries may exploit a software vulnerability to execute code or actions with higher privileges than intended.

techniques.name: Data from Information Repositories
techniques.description: Adversaries may leverage information repositories and APIs to mine data — for a web app, reading other users' records through IDOR / broken object-level authorization.

techniques.name: Data from Local System
techniques.description: Adversaries may search and collect files from a local system — reachable in a web context through path traversal, LFI or XXE that returns file contents.

techniques.name: Automated Collection
techniques.description: Adversaries may use automation to collect data, e.g. iterating every object id exposed by an IDOR to harvest a whole table.

techniques.name: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
techniques.description: Adversaries may communicate using HTTP/S to blend with normal traffic; an SSRF that reaches attacker infrastructure or a webhook that can be pointed outward enables this.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Web Service
techniques.description: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to an external web service; a blind SSRF or XXE that can send request bodies outbound is a channel for this.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
techniques.description: Adversaries may exfiltrate data over a protocol other than the existing C2 channel, e.g. an out-of-band XXE or SSRF using DNS or a secondary HTTP endpoint.

techniques.name: Endpoint Denial of Service
techniques.description: Adversaries may perform endpoint denial of service to degrade or block availability — ReDoS, an XML entity-expansion bomb, or an unbounded expensive operation.

techniques.name: Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
techniques.description: Adversaries may exhaust a service's resources by flooding it with requests or connections it cannot shed.

techniques.name: Network Denial of Service
techniques.description: Adversaries may perform network denial of service to degrade availability of a targeted service by saturating the network.

techniques.name: Data Manipulation
techniques.description: Adversaries may insert, delete or manipulate data to influence an outcome — e.g. a broken-access-control write that alters an order price or another user's record.

techniques.name: Data Manipulation: Stored Data Manipulation
techniques.description: Adversaries may alter data at rest to influence business processes or hide activity.

techniques.name: Data Destruction
techniques.description: Adversaries may destroy data — a broken-access-control or injection bug that permits arbitrary DELETE is the web-app path to this.

techniques.name: Network Service Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may enumerate services running on remote hosts; an SSRF that returns differentiable responses lets an attacker port-scan the internal network.

techniques.name: File and Directory Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may enumerate files and directories — an exposed directory listing or a path-traversal primitive used to map the filesystem.

techniques.name: Account Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may get a list of valid accounts — a login, registration or password-reset endpoint whose response distinguishes existing from non-existing users.

techniques.name: Active Scanning
techniques.description: Adversaries may execute active reconnaissance scans against a target's infrastructure to gather information for targeting.

techniques.name: Active Scanning: Vulnerability Scanning
techniques.description: Adversaries may scan a target to find vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting — e.g. identifying an outdated component with a known CVE.

techniques.name: Gather Victim Host Information
techniques.description: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's hosts — a stack trace, a debug page, or a verbose header that leaks the software and version in use.

techniques.name: Data from Information Repositories: Code Repositories
techniques.description: Adversaries may mine source code repositories — an exposed .git directory or published source maps disclose application source.

techniques.name: User Execution
techniques.description: Adversaries may rely on a user taking an action — clicking a link or submitting a form. CSRF, clickjacking and open-redirect abuse all require victim interaction.

techniques.name: Drive-by Compromise
techniques.description: Adversaries may gain access to a system through a user visiting a website — stored XSS that runs in every visitor's browser is a drive-by vector.

techniques.name: Content Injection
techniques.description: Adversaries may inject malicious content into traffic — HTTP response splitting, CRLF injection or web cache poisoning that serves attacker content to other users.

techniques.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
techniques.description: Adversaries may position between two systems to intercept or manipulate traffic — missing TLS, absent HSTS, or a downgrade path enables this against a web application.

techniques.name: Weaken Encryption
techniques.description: Adversaries may compromise a system's cryptography — a JWT accepting 'alg:none', a predictable session token, or a weak password hash.

techniques.name: Forge Web Credentials
techniques.description: Adversaries may forge web credentials — signing their own JWT with a leaked/guessable key, forging a SAML assertion, or predicting a session identifier.

techniques.name: Data from Configuration Repository
techniques.description: Adversaries may collect data from configuration repositories — an exposed framework actuator, or SSRF that reaches a cloud metadata endpoint.

techniques.name: Create Account
techniques.description: Adversaries may create an account to maintain access — a registration flow that lets a caller pick their role or verification state enables a privileged account.
